title: Heat Pump Rebates: What Survived, and Who No Longer Qualifies
summary: A 2026 explainer says the $2,000 federal credit ended in 2025 and a May 2026 DOE notice limited the HEEHR heat pump rebate to replacing electric equipment, while the fuel-neutral HOMES rebate still applies.

assertions.quote: The $2,000 credit for a heat pump ran out at the end of December.

verdicts.note: The paper refers to claiming a $2,000 IRA tax credit for a heat pump in 2023, consistent with the cap; it does not state the 30% rate.
IRS 25C page: from 2023 the credit equals 30% of qualified expenses, with a $2,000-per-year cap for qualified heat pumps (installation labor included).

assertions.quote: Set that against what died in December. $2,000 a year for a heat pump

verdicts.note: IRS fact sheet on the 2025 budget law (OBBB): the 25C home improvement credit is not allowed for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, and the 25D clean energy credit for expenditures after that date, so no federal heat pump credit applies to 2026 installs.
IRS 25C page: the credit applies to improvements made through December 31, 2025; nothing is available for 2026 installs.

assertions.quote: Between 80 and 150%, it covers half. Above that, nothing at all.

verdicts.note: The $4.5B IRA electrification rebates could cover roughly 500,000 low-income or 1 million moderate-income households, and efficiency rebates 0.5-2 million more, a small fraction of over 110 million households.

DOE Program Notice 26-2: the federal electrification rebate no longer funds replacing non-electric (gas, oil, propane) heating, which rules out most homes that would switch to a heat pump; it is also an income-limited program run by the states.
The DOE home energy rebates target low- to moderate-income households, and as of Feb 2026 most states had no launch date, so they are not available to most homeowners.

assertions.quote: 12 states and the District of Columbia had launched as of June. 43 states and territories still have none.

verdicts.note: As of Feb 2026, the National Housing Trust tracker shows most states' HEAR and HER programs only conditionally approved with no expected launch date (e.g. Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas), and others partly launched or in pilots, three-plus years after the 2022 law.

assertions.quote: Rebates are now allowed only for upgrading from existing electric equipment

verdicts.note: The source cites a May 2026 DOE program notice that could not be independently checked.

DOE Program Notice 26-2 (effective May 29, 2026) removes fuel-switching from the HEEHR (formerly HEAR) rebate, allowing HVAC rebates only for replacing existing electric equipment; launched programs must comply within three months, though existing reservations can still be honored.

North Carolina's state energy office: under DOE's May 29, 2026 guidance, from Sept. 1, 2026 HEAR rebates are no longer allowed for replacing gas or other fossil-fuel appliances; only electric-to-electric upgrades qualify.

assertions.quote: There is no fuel test in the whole house program because it was never built around fuel.

verdicts.note: HOMES is fuel-neutral and performance-based by design, but state availability and any 2026 changes are unverified.

assertions.quote: utilize rebates for insulation and air sealing prior to installing heating and cooling upgrades
